title: When an individual story becomes a racial pattern
interpretation: A defensible initial story does not settle whether selection, repeated framing, prominence and persistence produce unequal treatment. Structural bias can be examined without an editor admitting intent. A deliberate strategy to conceal bias is a separate claim requiring evidence.

studies.label: Cardiff REACH media monitoring report (2011)
studies.text: Cardiff REACH report (2011): 66.9% of 499 sampled items featuring Black males aged11–24 were crime-related, compared with41.9% for all young men/boys, not white-only. Eight two-week monitoring windows,2008–09; news in print, TV and radio. Victims were included. This is historical content analysis, not a measure of the present cases or evidence of each editor’s intent.
studies.finding: Crime accounted for 66.9% of sampled items featuring Black young men and boys, against 41.9% for all young men and boys.
studies.limit: The comparator includes Black youth; the sample is from 2008–09 and includes victims. It does not mean 67% portrayed Black people as criminals.

studies.label: Black British Voices Project (2023)
studies.text: Cambridge/Voice/I-Cubed Black British Voices (2023), over10,000 respondents: three in four believed Black businesses were treated unfairly by investors and financial institutions. The report describes perceived media stereotyping and football double standards. Survey/interviews are evidence of respondents’ experiences and perceptions, not a content audit or a causal finding for these cases.
studies.finding: Three in four respondents believed Black businesses were treated unfairly by investors and financial institutions. Media stereotyping and football double standards were also concerns in the report.
studies.limit: A survey and interviews document reported experience and perceptions. Business-investment findings cannot be relabelled as a measured media-coverage disparity.
studies.locator: Business/enterprise and media chapters; University of Cambridge summary.

industrySource.label: NCTJ Diversity in Journalism (2023)
industrySource.finding: Its 2022 data estimated that 88% of UK journalists were White. Workforce representation is relevant context; this statistic alone does not demonstrate a newsroom’s bias.

attributionCorrections: The crime statistic is from Cardiff’s REACH report, not a verified Reuters study.
The Lammy Review concerns criminal-justice disparities. The cited wealth-and-driving claim is not established by that review; separate Liberty/StopWatch work addresses traffic stops.
questions: Did criticism of a specific act become a fixed judgment about the whole person?
Did money, dress, cars or ambition become a reason to portray someone as undeserving?
Was an allegation repeatedly recalled after its status changed, without new information?
Were replies, achievements and ordinary context given similar prominence?
Would the same conduct, evidence and public role have attracted similar persistence and framing for someone else?
claimBoundary: Neither serious allegations nor proven wrongdoing gives an outlet unlimited permission for humiliation. Fair scrutiny of alleged abuse also protects complainants; the question is how the coverage treats evidence, power and people.
